title: Low Calcium, High PTH: CKD, PTH Assays and PTH Resistance
summary: Learn how kidney disease drives secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, what each generation of PTH assay actually measures, and how to tell secondary disease from pseudohypoparathyroidism and magnesium-deficiency hypocalcaemia.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 16 Hits 9–10 and Exam Traps 4–5, checked against KDIGO 2017, Kritmetapak 2019, Chandran 2019, Salera 2025, Mantovani 2018 (PHP consensus) and Albert 2025 (all full text via Europe PMC). Qualified: the reviewer calls biointact (1–84) assays “essential” in renal failure; the sources say third-generation assays also detect an N-terminal PTH form, show little added clinical value, and KDIGO 2017 keeps intact PTH in routine use (rv-biointact-pth-routine). The reviewer’s PTH-infusion cAMP test is described by the PHP consensus as not necessary for diagnosis, and PHP type 2 has a normal cAMP rise (rv-php-camp-infusion). Not taught: the reviewer’s intact PTH interval 10–65 pg/mL (assay-specific).

objectives: Explain how phosphate retention, FGF23 and low 1,25(OH)2D drive secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD, and what tertiary hyperparathyroidism adds.
Describe what first-, second- and third-generation PTH assays detect and why results differ in CKD.
Distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism and magnesium-deficiency hypocalcaemia from calcium, phosphate, PTH and magnesium.

scenes.title: Three high-PTH puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients with hypocalcaemia. (1) An adult on haemodialysis: calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high. (2) A 10-year-old with short fourth metacarpals and a round face: calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high, but kidney function, magnesium and 25(OH)D normal. (3) An adult with chronic diarrhoea: calcium low, magnesium 0.35 mmol/L, PTH inappropriately normal; calcium infusion helps only briefly. Question token: “Shouting gland, deaf tissue, or muted gland?”

cues.text: Three patients, all with low calcium. A dialysis patient with high phosphate and high PTH. A ten-year-old with short fourth fingers, high phosphate and high PTH, but normal kidneys.
And an adult with chronic diarrhoea, very low magnesium, and a PTH that is not raised at all.
Same low calcium, three different PTH problems. Which is which?

props.label: Shouting gland, deaf tissue, or muted gland?

scenes.title: How CKD drives secondary hyperparathyroidism
scenes.altText: Schematic chain: failing kidney → phosphate retained; FGF23 and PTH rise first and keep phosphate normal until about CKD G4 → phosphate and FGF23 inhibit renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase → less 1,25(OH)2D → less gut calcium absorption and hypocalcaemia → parathyroids secrete more PTH and enlarge (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Glands progress from diffuse to nodular hyperplasia with fewer calcium-sensing and vitamin D receptors. Tertiary card: after longstanding secondary disease, glands become quasi-autonomous and calcium rises. Footnote: bone histology (renal osteodystrophy) is classified by biopsy with the turnover, mineralization and volume (TMV) system.

cues.text: In chronic kidney disease, the kidney cannot excrete phosphate. FGF23 and PTH rise early and push phosphate out, so serum phosphate often stays normal until about stage four.

Phosphate and FGF23 both block the kidney enzyme one-alpha-hydroxylase, so active vitamin D falls. Less calcium is absorbed, calcium falls, and the parathyroids make more PTH. That is secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Over time the glands grow, first diffusely, then as nodules with fewer calcium-sensing and vitamin D receptors. After long-standing disease they can act almost autonomously and calcium rises: tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
The bone damage itself, renal osteodystrophy, is classified on bone biopsy by turnover, mineralization and volume: the TMV system.

scenes.title: Which PTH does the assay see?
scenes.altText: Schematic PTH(1-84) bar with antibody epitopes. First generation: C-terminal radioimmunoassay, detects intact PTH plus C-terminal fragments that accumulate in CKD; replaced by second-generation sandwich assays. Second generation (“intact PTH”): capture antibody against 39-84, detection antibody against an N-terminal region (12-18, 13-24 or 26-32); also detects non-(1-84) fragments such as PTH(7-84), which can make up to about half of measured PTH in CKD. Third generation (“biointact”, “whole” or “bioactive”): detection antibody against amino acids 1-4, so 7-84 is not detected; it does detect an N-terminal PTH form and reads roughly 50-70% of intact-assay values in CKD. KDIGO 2017 token: intact PTH remains in routine use; dialysis target about 2-9 times the upper limit of the assay used; decide on trends.

cues.text: PTH is eighty-four amino acids long, and the activity sits at the amino end. First-generation assays used antibodies against the carboxyl end, so they also counted inactive fragments that pile up in kidney failure.

Second-generation, so-called intact PTH assays, pair a carboxyl-end capture antibody with an amino-end detection antibody. But they also detect long fragments such as PTH seven to eighty-four, which can make up to about half the measured PTH in kidney disease.

Third-generation, biointact or whole PTH assays, detect the first four amino acids, so seven to eighty-four is missed. They are not perfectly specific either: they also see an amino-terminal PTH form, and in kidney disease they read roughly fifty to seventy percent of intact values.
KDIGO 2017 keeps intact PTH in routine use. For dialysis patients it suggests about two to nine times the upper limit of the assay used, and decisions based on trends, not one value.

props.title: 2nd gen: “intact” PTH
lines: Up to ~50% of result in CKD

scenes.title: Reading calcium, phosphate and PTH together
scenes.altText: Pattern table. Primary hyperparathyroidism: calcium high, phosphate low, PTH high. Secondary (CKD): calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high. Tertiary: calcium high, phosphate high, PTH high. Pseudohypoparathyroidism: hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and high PTH with normal kidney function and magnesium and no vitamin D deficiency (PTH resistance); confirm with molecular genetic testing. Low magnesium: hypocalcaemia with low or inappropriately normal PTH plus tissue resistance to PTH; calcium and vitamin D alone do not correct it; replace magnesium. Hook answers: (1) secondary hyperparathyroidism of CKD; (2) pseudohypoparathyroidism; (3) hypomagnesaemia.

cues.text: Read calcium, phosphate and PTH together. Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate, high PTH. Secondary, in kidney disease: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH. Tertiary: calcium and phosphate both high, with high PTH.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism looks like hypoparathyroidism, low calcium and high phosphate, but PTH is high: the tissues resist it. The consensus definition needs normal kidney function and magnesium and no vitamin D deficiency, and genetic testing confirms it.
Severe magnesium deficiency does two things: it suppresses PTH secretion and blunts tissue response to PTH. Calcium and vitamin D alone will not fix it; magnesium must be replaced.
Hook answers: the dialysis patient has secondary hyperparathyroidism, the child has pseudohypoparathyroidism, and the adult with diarrhoea has hypomagnesaemia.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Any PTH assay works in kidney failure” (✓ intact assays also detect 7-84 fragments and assays disagree; judge against the upper limit of the assay used and follow trends); “Low calcium with high PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism” (✓ primary has HIGH calcium; low calcium with high PTH is secondary hyperparathyroidism or PTH resistance); “Give more calcium for refractory hypocalcaemia” (✓ check magnesium; low magnesium suppresses PTH and blunts its action).

cues.text: Trap one: any PTH assay works in kidney failure. No: intact assays also count seven to eighty-four fragments, and assays disagree. Judge each result against the upper limit of the assay used, and follow the trend.
Trap two: low calcium with high PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism. No: primary disease raises calcium. Low calcium with high PTH is secondary disease or PTH resistance.
Trap three: hypocalcaemia keeps coming back, so give more calcium. No: check magnesium first.

props.title: ✗ “Any PTH assay works in CKD.”
lines: ✓ Assays disagree; use that assay’s ULN and trends

scenes.title: Shout, deaf, mute
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SHOUT, DEAF, MUTE. In kidney disease the gland SHOUTS (secondary) and may never stop (tertiary). In pseudohypoparathyroidism the tissues are DEAF to PTH. In magnesium deficiency the gland is MUTE.” Tokens: shout = CKD · deaf = pseudohypoparathyroidism · mute = low magnesium. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: shout, deaf, mute. In kidney disease the gland shouts, and after years it may never stop. In pseudohypoparathyroidism the tissues are deaf to PTH. In magnesium deficiency the gland goes mute.

Where it breaks: kidney disease also makes bone partly deaf to PTH; low magnesium both mutes the gland and deafens the tissues; and in pseudohypoparathyroidism PTH resistance develops over childhood, so early calcium may be normal.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: CKD bone is also partly resistant
Low Mg: mute gland AND deaf tissue

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Low Ca + high phosphate + high PTH: CKD (secondary) or PTH resistance · low Mg mutes PTH”, “Intact PTH also counts 7-84 fragments → that assay’s upper limit, trends”.

cues.text: Low calcium with high PTH means secondary hyperparathyroidism or PTH resistance, low magnesium can silence PTH, and in kidney disease PTH must be read against the upper limit of the assay used and followed as a trend because intact assays also count inactive fragments.

explanation.what: Plain language: when the kidneys fail, phosphate builds up and active vitamin D falls, so calcium drops and the parathyroid glands work overtime; after years they can keep working even when calcium is high. PTH tests do not all measure the same molecules, and low calcium with high PTH can also mean the body ignores PTH, while very low magnesium stops the glands from responding. Scientific terms: secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, FGF23, 1-alpha-hydroxylase, nodular hyperplasia, calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), vitamin D receptor (VDR), renal osteodystrophy, TMV classification, intact (second-generation) PTH, biointact or whole (third-generation) PTH(1-84), non-(1-84) PTH fragments such as PTH(7-84), pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP), Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO), Gs-alpha, hypomagnesaemia.
explanation.why: Phosphate retention and FGF23 lower calcitriol and calcium and stimulate PTH; long-standing stimulation produces nodular glands with fewer CaSR and VDR, which can become quasi-autonomous. Intact PTH assays cross-react with non-(1-84) fragments that accumulate when clearance falls, so values depend on the assay. In PHP, defective PTH receptor signalling causes the hypoparathyroid pattern with high PTH. Magnesium is needed both for PTH secretion and for its target-tissue action.
explanation.measure: Pattern (Ca · phosphate · PTH): primary ↑ ↓ ↑; secondary in CKD ↓ ↑ ↑; tertiary ↑ ↑ ↑. KDIGO 2017: in CKD G5D suggest intact PTH about 2–9 times the upper normal limit of the assay; base decisions on trends and serial calcium, phosphate and PTH together. Third-generation results are roughly 50–70% of intact-assay results in CKD. PHP: hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and high PTH with normal renal function and magnesium and no vitamin D deficiency; molecular genetic testing confirms. Symptomatic hypomagnesaemia usually appears around 0.5 mmol/L or lower.
explanation.differs: Second-generation (detects PTH(1-84) plus 7-84 fragments) vs third-generation (detection at amino acids 1–4; misses 7-84 but detects an N-terminal PTH form); secondary (low or normal calcium) vs tertiary (high calcium); PHP (high PTH, tissue resistance) vs magnesium deficiency (low or inappropriately normal PTH plus resistance) vs hypoparathyroidism (low PTH).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a dialysis patient with discordant PTH results between assays, a hypocalcaemic child with high PTH and AHO features, or refractory hypocalcaemia that needs magnesium.

mnemonic.text: SHOUT, DEAF, MUTE: in kidney disease the gland SHOUTS (secondary) and may never stop (tertiary); in pseudohypoparathyroidism the tissues are DEAF to PTH; in magnesium deficiency the gland is MUTE.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates excess secretion, tissue resistance and failed secretion as causes of abnormal calcium handling.
mnemonic.limitation: CKD also causes partial skeletal resistance to PTH; magnesium deficiency causes both impaired secretion and tissue resistance; in pseudohypoparathyroidism PTH resistance develops over childhood, so calcium can be normal early.

questions.stem: A haemodialysis patient’s PTH is measured on the same sample by a second-generation (intact) assay and a third-generation (biointact) assay. The intact result is clearly higher. What best explains this?

options.text: The intact assay also detects non-(1-84) fragments such as PTH(7-84), which accumulate in kidney failure
options.rationale: Correct. Intact assays cross-react with long amino-truncated fragments; third-generation assays target amino acids 1–4 and do not detect them.

options.text: The biointact assay detects C-terminal fragments the intact assay misses
options.rationale: Incorrect. Detecting C-terminal fragments is a first-generation assay problem; it would raise, not lower, the result.

options.text: PTH(1-84) has a half-life of several hours in kidney failure
options.rationale: Incorrect. Intact PTH clears within minutes; it is the C-terminal fragments that persist for hours.

options.text: The biointact assay measures only oxidized PTH
options.rationale: Incorrect. Intact and bioactive assays both measure oxidized and non-oxidized PTH.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with short stature and short fourth metacarpals has low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH. Kidney function, magnesium and 25(OH)D are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. Hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia with high PTH, normal renal function and magnesium, and no vitamin D deficiency define PTH resistance; AHO features fit.
Incorrect. The calcium and phosphate pattern matches, but PTH would be low, not high.
Incorrect. Primary disease raises calcium and lowers phosphate.

questions.stem: An adult with chronic diarrhoea has symptomatic hypocalcaemia, serum magnesium 0.35 mmol/L and an inappropriately normal PTH. Intravenous calcium helps only briefly. What is the best next step?

options.rationale: Correct. Severe magnesium deficiency impairs PTH secretion and target-tissue response; calcium and vitamin D alone do not correct it.

options.text: Give more calcium and add cholecalciferol
options.rationale: Incorrect. Without magnesium, the hypocalcaemia stays refractory.

options.text: Order a PTH infusion test for pseudohypoparathyroidism
options.rationale: Incorrect. The PHP definition requires normal magnesium, and PTH here is not raised.

options.text: Repeat PTH on a third-generation assay
options.rationale: Incorrect. The assay is not the problem; magnesium deficiency is suppressing PTH.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 16 Hit 10 calls biointact (1–84) PTH assays “essential” in chronic renal failure and Trap 4 says to use one “for the true value”. Kritmetapak 2019 reports that third-generation assays also detect an N-terminal PTH form and that KDIGO 2017 keeps second-generation (intact) assays in routine use; Chandran 2019 notes little evidence that they add clinical information. KDIGO 2017 targets are multiples of the assay’s own upper limit, with decisions on trends (register flag rv-biointact-pth-routine).

Ch. 16 Trap 5 cites a subnormal urinary cAMP response to PTH infusion for pseudohypoparathyroidism. The 2018 international consensus (Mantovani 2018) states exogenous PTH testing is not necessary for diagnosis, confirms PHP by molecular genetic analysis, and notes PHP type 2 shows a cAMP rise with a deficient phosphaturic response (register flag rv-php-camp-infusion).

Ch. 16 Hit 10 gives intact PTH normal as 10–65 pg/mL. PTH reference intervals are assay-specific; KDIGO 2017 expresses targets relative to the upper normal limit of the assay used. The interval is not taught.
